title: Write a search procedure
summary: Write a traversal and justify the data structure that holds its frontier.
cues: A traversal must be written or completed for a graph

workflow.why: The frontier's order is the search order.

cases.when: The oldest discovered node is explored first
cases.then: Keep the frontier in a queue (breadth-first)

cases.when: The newest discovered node is explored first
cases.then: Keep the frontier in a stack (depth-first)

workflow.do: Start, then loop: take, expand, record

apply.text: Mark a node when it enters the frontier, so it is never added twice.

symbols.meaning: nodes reachable from the start node

blocks.title: Task
paragraphs: Breadth-first search from S: say which structure holds the frontier, then write the search.

blocks.title: Graph
blocks.description: An undirected graph: S links to A and B, and A links to C.

blocks.title: Solution
paragraphs: A queue holds the frontier. Put S in; then repeatedly take the oldest node, visit its unseen neighbours and add them.

steps.prompt: Which node does breadth-first search explore next: the oldest or the newest it has found?
case_feedback: Yes: breadth-first takes the oldest discovered node, so the frontier is first in, first out.
Taking the newest node first goes deep along one branch; that is depth-first.

steps.prompt: Write `bfs(graph, start)`. `graph` maps each node to a list of its neighbours.

answer.title: Search

blocks.title: Task
paragraphs: List the order in which nodes are taken from S: (a) breadth-first, (b) depth-first. Add a node's neighbours in alphabetical order.

blocks.title: Graph
blocks.description: An undirected graph: S links to A and B, and A links to C.

blocks.title: Orders
blocks.caption: The stack takes B first because it was pushed last.

case_feedback: Yes: breadth-first explores the oldest discovered node, so the frontier is a queue.

answer.title: Frontier
paragraphs: A queue: first in, first out.

steps.prompt: Take, expand and record until the queue is empty. In which order are the nodes taken?

check.feedback: S, then its neighbours A and B in order, then C.

case_feedback: Yes: depth-first explores the newest discovered node, so the frontier is a stack.

answer.title: Frontier
paragraphs: A stack: last in, first out.

steps.prompt: Take, expand and record until the stack is empty. In which order are the nodes taken?

check.feedback: S pushes A, then B; B is on top, so it is taken before A.

pitfalls.situation: Deciding where to mark nodes as seen in the BFS loop.
pitfalls.why: A node marked only when taken can be added twice while it waits, so it is visited twice.

drill.prompt: A crawler fetches pages in the order it found their links. Which structure holds the pages still to fetch?

blocks.title: Links found
blocks.caption: news and shop were found before sport.

drill.explanation: The oldest found page is fetched next: a queue, as in breadth-first search.

guide.prompt: After fetching news, which waiting page was found first?
guide.hint: Compare when shop and sport entered the frontier.

paragraphs: shop entered before sport. Taking the oldest waiting page requires a FIFO queue.

drill.prompt: Search the graph depth-first from A, adding neighbours in alphabetical order. In which order are the nodes taken?

blocks.title: Graph
blocks.description: A links to B and C; B links to D.

drill.explanation: The newest node is taken first, so the search finishes C before it returns to B.

solution.title: Stack
solution.caption: Order taken: A, C, B, D.

guide.prompt: When B then C are pushed, which node does a stack take next?
guide.hint: The last pushed node is on top.

paragraphs: C is taken next, because it was pushed after B.

guide.prompt: Continue the stack until no node remains.
guide.hint: Mark each node when pushed and skip neighbours already seen.

paragraphs: Take A, then C, then B, then D. After each expansion the stacks are [B, C], [B], [D], then empty.
